nameStory: The butterfish gets its slippery name from its incredibly smooth, almost buttery skin that makes it nearly impossible to grip with bare hands. When you catch one, it literally slides through your fingers like a bar of wet soap! This silvery fish feels so slick and smooth that early fishermen thought it was as slippery as melted butter.
description: The butterfish is a small, silvery ocean fish with an oval, flattened body that's perfectly built for life in open water. These smooth-skinned swimmers typically grow to about 6-9 inches long and have a distinctive compressed, almost pancake-like shape when viewed head-on. Their bodies shine with a bright silver color and feel remarkably slippery to the touch, making them one of the most distinctive fish you'll encounter in New England waters. Butterfish are schooling fish that travel in large groups through coastal waters.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deeply compressed, oval body that feels flat and pancake-like when held sideways, with a smooth, streamlined profile perfect for open water swimming

idTips.label: Skin Texture
idTips.description: Extraordinarily slippery, smooth skin that feels like wet soap or melted butter - you literally cannot grip this fish with bare hands

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright silvery body with a metallic sheen that flashes in sunlight, sometimes with faint darker spots along the back

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, flowing dorsal and anal fins that run almost the entire length of the body, giving it a ribbon-like appearance when swimming

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish typically 6-9 inches long, easily fitting in your palm if you could actually hold onto one

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth positioned at the front of the head, designed for eating small prey like jellyfish and plankton

habitat: Butterfish live in the open waters of the Atlantic Ocean along New England's coast, typically swimming in schools in the upper water column. You'll encounter them in offshore waters and sometimes closer to shore during certain seasons, usually in depths ranging from shallow coastal waters to several hundred feet deep. They prefer the open ocean environment rather than rocky bottoms or structured habitats.

seasonality.spring: Butterfish begin moving into New England waters as temperatures warm, often appearing in catches as they follow plankton blooms northward along the coast.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for butterfish in New England waters, when they're most abundant and actively feeding in large schools throughout coastal areas.
seasonality.fall: Butterfish remain common but begin their southward migration as water temperatures start to cool, making this a good time for shore-based encounters.
seasonality.winter: Most butterfish have migrated south to warmer waters, though some may linger in deeper offshore areas where temperatures remain more stable.

funFact: Butterfish are so slippery that commercial fishermen often have to use special gloves or towels just to handle them, and they can actually squeeze through fishing net holes that seem too small for their body size by compressing their flexible, cartilage-rich frame!
confusionNotes: Butterfish are most easily confused with small pompanos or young scup, but the butterfish's impossibly slippery skin is the dead giveaway - no other New England fish feels quite so much like trying to hold onto a greased marble.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "butterfish," this species is completely unrelated to the butterfish found in other parts of the world or in freshwater - it's a uniquely Atlantic Ocean species that just happens to share the slippery, buttery name.
compareHints: Butterfish can be distinguished from their close relative the harvestfish by their more northern range and slightly different fin proportions. Harvestfish are more commonly found in southern waters and have a slightly deeper body profile, while butterfish have the more elongated fins and are the primary butterfish species you'll encounter in New England waters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the butterfish, harvestfish are much more circular and deep-bodied rather than oval-shaped.
